strengths: The paper introduces an innovative paradigm that shifts from per-sample, inference-time tool generation to offline, task-wise visual prompt exploration, effectively amortizing search costs and resulting in dramatically faster and cheaper inference compared to methods like SketchPad.

The technical formulation of SEVEX is well-conceived, particularly the decoupling of the abstract idea space from low-level programmatic implementation, the Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) balancing exploration and parent-branch saturation, and the semantic backpropagation of sample-wise failure analyses.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on challenging perception-centric benchmarks (BlindTest and BLINK) demonstrates clear gains in accuracy (+7.3% over Naive and +14.3% over SketchPad on average) with significantly fewer test tokens.

The investigation into prompt non-transferability across distinct LVLM backbones (Gemini, Claude, GPT-4o) provides valuable empirical evidence demonstrating that perceptual biases are architecture-specific, reinforcing the necessity for automated per-model discovery systems.
weaknesses: The main benchmark comparisons (Tables 2 and 3) are evaluated exclusively on Gemini-2.5-flash. While the non-transferability experiment (Table 4) includes Claude and GPT-4o on a single task, evaluating the full SEVEX discovery pipeline across multiple open-source and proprietary backbones across all tasks would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

The set of available visual tools includes powerful external expert models (GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, DepthAnything) alongside basic geometric drawing and cropping functions. It is somewhat difficult to disentangle how much of the performance gain stems from invoking external perception models versus pure visual scaffolding/formatting.

The evaluation is restricted to puzzle- and perception-heavy tasks from BlindTest and subsets of BLINK. Assessing the framework on broader multimodal benchmarks (e.g., MathVista, ChartQA, or fine-grained visual question answering) would better demonstrate generalizability across diverse multimodal reasoning domains.

While the token cost per iteration is documented in Table 3, a more comprehensive breakdown of the total computational overhead (wall-clock time, dollar cost, and execution failure/exception rates during Python code execution) would provide a clearer operational picture of the discovery phase.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: While programmatic visual prompting (visual scaffolding) can significantly alleviate LVLM perception failures, manual trial-and-error is unscalable and per-sample code generation (e.g., SketchPad) is computationally expensive and prone to compounding errors. Automating task-wise visual prompt discovery offers an effective amortized approach.

Technically sound exploration algorithm: Decoupling the high-level semantic idea space from low-level code implementation effectively addresses long-context distraction. The combination of Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) and qualitative Semantic Backpropagation ensures both breadth and depth in prompt exploration.

Compelling qualitative discoveries: SEVEX discovers clever, non-trivial strategies beyond conventional heuristics (e.g., repurposing DepthAnything to detect unnatural boundary discontinuities for Jigsaw puzzles, and drawing typographic reference lines to disambiguate character case).

Insightful analysis of non-transferability: The empirical demonstration that visual prompts do not transfer cleanly across different model architectures (Gemini, Claude, GPT-4o) provides a strong justification for automated, model-specific discovery frameworks.

Strong experimental performance: Significant gains over Naive inference and SketchPad baselines across 9 tasks on BlindTest and BLINK, with an order-of-magnitude reduction in test-time token costs compared to per-sample generation methods.
weaknesses: Limited task domain: The experimental evaluation focuses strictly on geometric and synthetic perception tasks from BlindTest and BLINK. Demonstrating how SEVEX generalizes to real-world visual understanding benchmarks (e.g., ChartQA, DocVQA, or fine-grained domain-specific perception tasks) would significantly strengthen the empirical claim.

Comparison to automated code/prompt optimization frameworks: The baseline comparison is mainly limited to SketchPad and an APE-augmented version. Comparison or discussion regarding broader optimization frameworks (e.g., DSPy-style multi-turn optimizers or TextGrad adapted to programmatic tools) would provide clearer positioning within the automated prompt engineering literature.

Small development set and variance: Using only 30 samples for exploration raises potential concerns about sensitivity to sample selection and overfitting on more diverse tasks. While the test results show good generalization here, reporting variance or error bars across the full benchmark suite would improve confidence in stability.

strengths: Novel perspective on visual prompting: Proposes an automated, offline task-level discovery framework (SEVEX) for programmatic visual prompts, contrasting with existing manual heuristic designs or expensive per-sample dynamic tool-use methods (e.g., SketchPad).

Principled search formulation: Decoupling the high-level semantic idea space from the low-level code implementation effectively reduces agent distraction and search space complexity. The Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) and semantic backpropagation provide a thoughtful adaptation of tree search to LLM-driven exploration.

Strong inference efficiency: By discovering a task-wise prompt during an offline exploration phase on a small development set (30 images), the method amortizes exploration costs and achieves test-time inference token counts that are orders of magnitude lower than per-sample reasoning frameworks like SketchPad.

Valuable empirical insight on non-transferability: The analysis in Section 4.5 clearly demonstrates that visual prompt strategies optimized for one LVLM architecture (e.g., Gemini) do not transfer reliably to others (e.g., Claude, GPT-4o), reinforcing the necessity of automated, model-specific optimization.
weaknesses: Restricted benchmark scope: Evaluation is confined to a subset of tasks from BlindTest and BLINK (synthetic/geometric perception and puzzle-like reasoning). It remains unclear how well SEVEX generalizes to broader multimodal benchmarks requiring fine-grained perception and real-world reasoning (e.g., ChartQA, InfoVQA, MathVista).

Heavy reliance on predefined tools and code synthesis: The expressiveness of discovered prompts is bounded by the predefined external toolset (GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, DepthAnything, OpenCV functions). The paper does not thoroughly analyze the failure modes or sensitivity when the Engineer agent produces buggy code or when relevant tools are absent.

Limited ablation coverage: Component ablations (w/o tree search, w/o semantic backpropagation, w/o abstract space) are reported on only two tasks (Jigsaw and Circle) due to computational constraints, making it harder to verify consistency across more complex multimodal settings.

Potential risk of overfitting on small dev sets: Exploring 50 iterations over a small 30-sample development set poses risk of overfitting prompt heuristics to specific dataset quirks, although the test set numbers show reasonable generalization for the evaluated tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely challenge: mitigating perception failures in LVLMs through automated visual prompting. Framing the discovery of visual prompts at the task level rather than via per-sample generation significantly reduces test-time latency and token overhead.

The proposed SEVEX algorithm is thoughtfully designed, decoupling abstract conceptual ideas from low-level code generation to avoid context distraction. The Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) formulation and semantic backpropagation mechanism offer a structured and principled exploration strategy.

Empirical evaluations across 9 challenging tasks from BlindTest and BLINK demonstrate significant performance gains over Naive inference and SketchPad/APE baselines, while achieving an order-of-magnitude reduction in test-time inference cost.

The paper provides insightful analyses, including search ablation studies, testing across three state-of-the-art backbones (Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet 4.0), and demonstrating the empirical non-transferability of visual prompts across LVLM architectures.
weaknesses: The task diversity is relatively constrained; the evaluation focuses on 4 tasks from BlindTest and 5 from BLINK. Demonstrating discovery on more mainstream visual reasoning or perception benchmarks (e.g., DocVQA, MathVista, or MM-Vet) would further strengthen claims of generality.

Upfront exploration cost is non-trivial: 50 search iterations over a 30-image development set involves 1,500 image evaluations plus multiple LLM agent calls (ideation, self-evaluation, engineering, and analysis). A clearer discussion on how search scale scales with task complexity or budget would be beneficial.

Comparison with simple text-only few-shot in-context learning (ICL) or multimodal Chain-of-Thought baselines on the same development set is missing, leaving open whether some gains could be achieved via standard few-shot prompting without visual scaffolding.

strengths: Conceptual formulation: Formulating visual prompt discovery as an automated task-wise tree search over an abstract idea space effectively decouples high-level semantic intent from low-level programmatic implementation, mitigating long-context code distraction for LLM agents.

Well-motivated algorithm design: Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) appropriately adapts Upper Confidence Bounds to expanding LLM-generated idea trees by accounting for heuristic novelty, sibling diversity, and parent saturation, complemented by semantic backpropagation of sample-wise failure analyses.

Inference and exploration efficiency: By discovering a task-level programmatic visual prompt offline on a small development set (30 images), SEVEX drastically cuts per-sample inference token costs by ~91% compared to test-time dynamic visual reasoning frameworks like SketchPad, while outperforming SketchPad+APE in search token efficiency.

Insightful analysis of visual prompt non-transferability: The empirical evaluation across three frontier models (Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4) clearly demonstrates that visual prompts do not transfer cleanly across backbones due to disparate perceptual biases, strongly justifying automated, model-specific discovery.

Informative ablations: The ablation studies validate each component of the tree search and semantic backpropagation, and the restricted-toolbox experiment confirms that the improvements stem primarily from the search strategy rather than mere reliance on heavy external vision tools.
weaknesses: Scope of evaluation benchmarks: Experiments are restricted to 4 synthetic/geometric tasks from BlindTest and 5 perception tasks from BLINK. Evaluating on broader visual understanding and reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MathVista, DocVQA, or real-world fine-grained recognition) would better establish the generalizability of task-wise visual scaffolding.

Dependence on proprietary agent models: The idea generation, implementation, and semantic analysis heavily rely on Gemini-2.5-flash with 'thinking' enabled. The paper does not explore whether open-weight models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder or Llama-3.1) can serve as effective engineers and analysts in this loop.

Robustness and execution overhead of code generation: Programmatic visual prompting involves generating and executing arbitrary Python scripts invoking CV tools. While a feasibility filter is mentioned, the paper lacks detailed statistics on execution error rates, sandbox timeouts, or syntax repair cycles encountered during the 50 search iterations.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: The search relies on multiple balancing coefficients (lambda_expl, lambda_novel, lambda_sat, branching factor k), but sensitivity analyses or guidelines for setting these hyperparameters across diverse task domains are not provided.

strengths: Well-motivated framing: While existing methods such as SketchPad rely on expensive per-instance code generation during inference or manual prompt engineering, this work formulates task-wise programmatic visual prompt discovery via agentic search, amortizing exploration cost over future inferences.

Sound methodological design: Searching over an abstract semantic idea space rather than low-level code effectively prevents distraction from syntactical and low-level execution details. The Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) and semantic backpropagation mechanism (distilling sample-wise failure modes into natural language insights) are well-crafted and logically sound.

Thorough empirical validation: Evaluated on challenging fine-grained perception benchmarks (BlindTest and BLINK), SEVEX consistently outperforms the Naive baseline and SketchPad, while reducing inference token overhead by over 90% relative to test-time code generation baselines.

Insightful findings on non-transferability: The empirical demonstration that visual prompts optimized for one LVLM backbone fail to transfer or even hurt performance on other backbones (Table 4) provides strong empirical justification for automated, model-specific discovery frameworks.

Comprehensive ablations: The paper provides meaningful ablations analyzing the necessity of the abstract idea space, tree search, semantic backpropagation, and the contribution of external tools vs. basic drawing primitives.
weaknesses: Limited benchmark breadth: The evaluation is concentrated on 9 tasks across BlindTest and BLINK. Evaluating on a broader variety of multimodal reasoning benchmarks (e.g., visual math, chart reasoning, or real-world spatial perception) would further demonstrate the generalizability of the proposed discovery pipeline.

Sensitivity to development set sample size and composition: The framework relies on a small 30-sample development set for guided exploration. Although split stability is analyzed for CircledLetter in the appendix, full cross-validation and variance analysis across all evaluated tasks are absent, leaving some concern regarding task-specific overfitting.

Tool vocabulary constraints: The expressive power of discovered visual prompts remains constrained by the predefined set of external models and graphic primitives in Table 1. Failure cases arising from missing functional primitives are not deeply characterized.

Exploration budget and computational overhead: Conducting 50 iterations of multi-agent ideation, tool execution, and sample-wise analysis on a dev set still requires a noticeable computational investment per task/model pair, which limits rapid ad-hoc deployment.
